title: Powerlifting centric Sheiko program review (part. 1, hypertrophy assessment)
summary: NH reviews viewer Griffin's Sheiko advanced program for hypertrophy. He criticizes block logic, pairing squat/bench and deadlift/bench on the same day, low reps, redundant posterior chain and shoulder work, and missing muscle groups (rows, biceps, calves, traps, neck, long head triceps), but judges the exercise pool redeemable and promises to rearrange it into a bodybuilding program.
claims: Strength work stays the pillar and foundation of hypertrophy training
Bodybuilders should not program in strict blocks; rotations and rep range changes create undulation within the program and keep tonnage stable
Tonnage stability is essential for hypertrophy but not for strength, where peaking forces low tonnage
Bodybuilders should never deload; it is a waste of time
Squat and bench on the same day waste time on warm-ups because they are unrelated body parts with no synergy; prefer upper/lower with variations
Staying in low reps on main lifts is not ideal for hypertrophy
3x5 on the deadlift sandbags; better a true top set with at most one rep in reserve, using 5-rep repeatable sets as back-off work
Bench and deadlift on the same day resembles a careless full body that just stacks every compound
For horizontal presses multiply both sets and reps since they tolerate high volume
Deadlifts to the knees make little sense since the sticking point for most is past the knees; do full reps unless using rack pulls or deficits for a specific purpose
If you cannot push every lift in a day to failure, even in higher reps, some of those exercises were unnecessary because the muscle was already fatigued
In good mornings the lower back stabilizes isometrically while the glutes and hamstrings move the bar; doing them with a fatigued lower back is how injuries happen
Do good mornings at the end of a day whose earlier knee flexion and hinges warmed the hamstrings and glutes without loading the lower back; do not pick them after heavy deadlifts
If benching 3x/week hurts your shoulders, swap in a shoulder-friendlier variation like close grip, slingshot or floor press
Back-off sets right after heavy work are the best way to accumulate tonnage on compounds because you are warm and fibers are pre-fatigued
Back-off reps: most reps and sets on bench, middle on squat, lower reps and more sets on deadlift
Regular back-offs may be better for hypertrophy than paused ones because of the stretch reflex, though I personally like pause work
Do abs until you cannot anymore, rest a minute and repeat instead of 3x10
Deficit deadlifts use more quad drive and are a good lift
Vertical presses matter for shoulder development; incline is only a hybrid
Incline bench followed by weighted dips over-fatigues the shoulders, and dips can be dangerous; pick one and push it
Deficit deadlifts and block pulls on the same day contradict each other; put them on different days
Back extensions on deadlift days are good; done cold they could be dangerous
Finishing a deadlift day with light hyperextensions teaches you to drive with the legs and reinforces a stable lower back
Overhead pressing at the end of horizontal press days teaches you to recruit all three delt heads and tuck the shoulders, and works injury-preventing muscles
Leg press on a deadlift day is a valid knee-flexion addition
Include long-head triceps work like overhead extensions or skull crushers
Overhead press once with 5x5 is not enough vertical press frequency or volume
A bodybuilding version needs rows, traps, wrist extensions, upper back, calves, biceps (curls, chin-ups) and neck work
Do not switch programs if you already have good neurological adaptation to the movements; rearrange them instead
exercises: end of day, after non-lumbar-taxing hinges; not after heavy deadlifts
